issues.legal_issue: Omitting a ground for eviction from the pre-suit notice does not by itself bar eviction on that ground when it is proved and legally available.
material_facts: The landlord's notice referred to expanding his own business but did not mention the need for space for an existing pawn-broking partnership business run by members of his family.
The eviction petition relied on the partnership business as well as the landlord's own business.
Evidence showed that the partnership business existed before the notice, was licensed and registered, and had been assessed for tax.
issues.conclusion: The omission raised suspicion but did not, by itself, make the claim mala fide or prevent the landlord from relying on the partnership business as a ground for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, bona fide requirement is assessed objectively on the evidence. Omission of a reasonable ground from the notice does not defeat an otherwise proved and legally permissible claim. The Court did not rely on an earlier case for this holding.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and eviction_ground_omitted_from_notice and ground_proved_on_evidence and ground_legally_available

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord seeks recovery of rented premises in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.eviction_ground_omitted_from_notice: The landlord's pre-suit notice did not state a ground later relied on in the eviction proceeding.
predicates.ground_proved_on_evidence: The landlord proves the later-asserted ground through evidence in the proceeding.
predicates.ground_legally_available: The later-asserted ground is one on which the governing law permits eviction.

issues.definition: When a landlord proves a legally available ground in a rent-control eviction case, omission of that ground from the notice alone does not prevent eviction on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A previous unsuccessful or inconsistent eviction history does not automatically defeat a later eviction claim based on a currently proved bona fide requirement.
material_facts: A previous tenant had been evicted on a ground relating to rebuilding, but the landlord did not rebuild the premises and later let them to another tenant.
The rebuilding ground was not accepted in the present proceeding.
The present claim relied on the requirement for an existing pawn-broking business, and the Court held that the claim had to be assessed on the evidence in the present proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The earlier conduct and the rejection of the rebuilding ground did not require the later eviction claim to be dismissed if the current bona fide requirement was established by cogent evidence.
issues.legal_principle: A cause for eviction based on bona fide requirement is recurring. A prior finding that a cause was not established, or a prior failure to rebuild after obtaining possession, does not foreclose a later claim founded on a subsequent cause or changed circumstances. Section 10(3)(a)(iii) governs the current business-requirement claim; rejection of a rebuilding claim under Section 14(1)(b) does not by itself bar a distinct, proved ground. The Court did not rely on an earlier case for this holding.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and later_eviction_claim and prior_eviction_history_or_inconsistent_conduct and current_bona_fide_ground_proved

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord seeks recovery of rented premises in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.later_eviction_claim: The landlord brings a later claim to recover premises from a tenant.
predicates.prior_eviction_history_or_inconsistent_c: The landlord previously pursued an eviction ground unsuccessfully or acted inconsistently with an earlier asserted ground.
predicates.current_bona_fide_ground_proved: The landlord establishes by cogent evidence a bona fide ground for eviction in the later proceeding.

issues.definition: A prior eviction history does not automatically defeat a later rent-control claim when the landlord proves a current bona fide ground.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court should not set aside a supported factual finding solely because the appellate authority did not describe each exhibit in detail when the record is available for review.
material_facts: After remand, the appellate authority referred to business records, including tax assessment materials, and found that the pawn-broking partnership business had been gradually expanding.
The High Court set aside that finding in part because the appellate authority had not identified and explained each exhibit in detail.
The exhibits were available to the High Court, and the Supreme Court considered the finding of expansion justified by the record.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted with hyper-technicality by discarding the appellate authority's supported finding without examining the available record.
issues.legal_principle: Where the record is available and an appellate authority has identified evidence supporting its factual finding, a revisional court should assess the evidence rather than reject the finding solely for lack of detailed exhibit descriptions. The Court did not invoke a statutory provision or earlier case for this holding.

rule.if: rent_control_revision and appellate_finding_supported_by_record and record_available_to_reviewing_court and finding_rejected_only_for_lack_of_exhibit_detail

predicates.rent_control_revision: A reviewing court is considering a revision arising from a rent-control eviction proceeding.
predicates.appellate_finding_supported_by_record: The appellate authority's factual finding is supported by evidence in the case record.
predicates.record_available_to_reviewing_court: The evidence relied on for the finding is available to the reviewing court.
predicates.finding_rejected_only_for_lack_of_exhibi: The reviewing court rejects the finding because the appellate authority did not describe the exhibits in sufficient detail.

issues.definition: When a supported finding and its evidence are available for review, rejecting the finding solely for insufficient exhibit detail is an improper hyper-technical reversal.

issues.legal_issue: When the actual space required for an expanding business has not been determined, the eviction appeal may be remanded for that limited assessment, with eviction to follow if bona fide need is found.
material_facts: The appellate authority found that the pawn-broking partnership business was expanding and needed to be run separately, but it had not determined the actual space required in light of the nature and extent of that business.
The parties had already adduced evidence after the first remand.

The Supreme Court directed that the assessment be made on the existing materials and allowed the tenant to offer additional evidence only if circumstances had changed so that the landlord had obtained suitable alternative accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the remand only to determine the actual space required for the partnership business. If the appellate authority found a bona fide need for the premises as a separate business enclosure, it was to order eviction; no further evidence was to be received except evidence of the specified subsequent change in circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 10(3)(a)(iii) of the Tamil Nadu Building (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, eviction for a non-residential business requirement depends on a bona fide need for the premises. The assessment must account for the nature and expansion of the business and the actual space required. Once the parties have had the opportunity to adduce evidence, the remand may be confined to the unresolved issue on the existing record, subject to evidence of a subsequent change in circumstances relevant to suitable alternative accommodation. The Court did not rely on an earlier case for this direction.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_appeal and business_expansion_supported_by_record and actual_space_requirement_unresolved and parties_already_led_evidence

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal: An appeal concerns a landlord's request to recover rented premises for a business requirement.
predicates.business_expansion_supported_by_record: Evidence supports the finding that the business for which the premises are sought is expanding.
predicates.actual_space_requirement_unresolved: The deciding authority has not determined how much space the business actually requires, considering its nature and expansion.
predicates.parties_already_led_evidence: Both sides have already had an opportunity to present evidence in the proceeding.

issues.definition: When an expanding business's actual space need remains undetermined after the parties have presented evidence, the appeal is remanded only for that assessment on the existing record.
